I've gathered what I need from the authoritative sources. One note first: **validatebp.org (the US registry) blocked me with a "Verify you are human" checkbox, which I don't click.** I worked around it using STRIDE BP (the ESH/ISH/World Hypertension League registry) and the AHA — but you'll want to do that final US-model lookup yourself.

## The single most important filter: independent validation

"FDA-cleared" is a regulatory step, not proof of accuracy. What you want is **independent clinical validation**, tracked by two registries: **validatebp.org** (US, AMA/AHA-backed) and **stridebp.org** (international).

I pulled STRIDE BP's home-monitoring list generated today (Sep 5, 2026): **335 validated upper-arm devices currently on the market**, plus 86 validated-but-discontinued ones.

## Use STRIDE BP's "Preferred" flag — it encodes your exact criteria

Their "Preferred device" ribbon requires *all* of the following:
- Upper-arm cuff
- ≥1 approved validation study published **within the last 10 years**
- Using a **recent protocol** (ISO 81060-2:2018 Universal Standard; ANSI/AAMI/ISO 2013 or 2009; ESH-IP 2010)
- **Automated storage of multiple readings, or phone/PC/internet connectivity** for data transfer

That bundles validated accuracy + correct form factor + data management into one filter. Filter to "Preferred" and you've done most of the work.

## Upper arm only — skip wrist and finger

Both sources are blunt. STRIDE BP lists wrist devices under: *"Generally not recommended due to inferior accuracy to upper-arm devices in practice and issues with correct use."* AHA: *"Wrist and finger monitors are not recommended. They give less reliable readings."*

## Cuff fit — measure your arm before you shop

This is the most commonly botched step, and a wrong cuff makes an otherwise-validated device inaccurate.

| Cuff | Arm circumference |
|---|---|
| Small adult | 22–26 cm (8.7–10.2 in) |
| Standard/medium | 27–34 cm (10.6–13.4 in) |
| Large adult | 35–44 cm (13.8–17.3 in) |

Many bundled "standard" cuffs only span 22–32 cm. An AHA news item (Sep 2024) noted that shifting the range to 25–45 cm would properly fit ~2.3 million more US adults. If you're near a boundary or above ~32 cm, buy a wide-range model or the correct separate cuff.

## Models carrying the Preferred flag today

Names below are STRIDE's (EU) naming — **US model numbers differ**, so verify your exact model:

- **Omron** — M3 Comfort (HEM-7155-E), M4 Intelli IT (HEM-7155T-EBK), M6 Comfort (HEM-7360-E), M7 Intelli IT (HEM-7361T-EBK), X7 Smart (HEM-7361T-ESL), Evolv (HEM-7600T), Complete (HEM-7530T-E3)
- **A&D** — UA-651Plus, UA-651SL Plus, UA-1200BLE, UA-1100NFC
- **Microlife** — BP A150 AFIB, BP A200 AFIB, BP A3 PC, BP A3L Comfort
- **Rossmax** — X3, X5, X9, Z1, Z5
- **Others** — Aponorm Basic/Professional Control, Hartmann Veroval, Qardio QardioArm, PIC solution OneRAPID

## Your buying sequence

1. Measure mid-upper-arm circumference with a tape.
2. Look up the **exact model number** on validatebp.org (US) or stridebp.org — not the product line name.
3. Confirm the included cuff's range covers your measurement.
4. Confirm memory storage + automatic averaging of consecutive readings, and that any app exports data (CSV/PDF) without a subscription.
5. Check it's on the "available on the market" list, not the discontinued one — matters for replacement cuffs over the device's life.
6. Per AHA: bring it to your next appointment so your clinician can check it against office equipment, and re-check roughly annually.

## Two things worth flagging

**On ease of use**, prioritize one-button operation, a large display, and an AC adapter option over feature count. On **data management**, built-in memory with two user profiles is the practical floor; Bluetooth is a convenience layer, not an accuracy feature.

**On marketing noise** — the top Google result for my registry search was a *sponsored ad* for a monitor advertising "FDA-Cleared Technology" and "Doctor-Ready Reports." I ignored it, and it's a good illustration of your instinct: ad copy and Amazon rankings don't track validation status. The registries do.

Staying within scope, this is device-selection guidance only — how often to measure and what any readings mean are conversations for your clinician.
